title: Chapter 224 – What Corin Remembered
html:
[Terrace Six – Hua]

Hua has never liked being the smallest person in a room, and on the Sixth Terrace there is no room, only a silver plain without a wall, and she is the smallest thing in it by a distance.

She sits cross-legged on the boards beside the iron stove with her cloth in her lap and her tea going cold in its gray clay cup, and watches the others sleep. It is not a thing she means to do. It is a thing she cannot stop. Pebble lies on his side with the red ribbon still wrapped around his wrist like a bracelet and his shaven head pillowed on a folded cloak. Jian sits upright against the beam, as he always does, with his steady hand open on his knee and his chin on his chest. Veyra stands at the edge of the light, as she always does, awake, a gray column against the silver dark.

And Yue lies on her back with her stone hand on her chest, and breathes very slowly, and her hair is white.

Not all of it. A single broad streak runs from the left temple to the nape of her neck, bright as new snow against the dark, exactly where the cut thread touched her in the instant the shears closed. It is the year. It is the thing the Loom took. Hua had watched it happen, from three paces away, and had thought she was seeing something gentler than it was: a quiet change of color, a shift of light. It had not looked like anything at all. And then Yue had lowered the shears, and swayed, and said oh, in a voice of mild surprise, and put a hand to her hair.

It suits you, Veyra had said.

I look like Mei.

She looks like you. The cool voice had been very dry. She wears it better.

Yue had laughed, a short startled bark, and sat down on the boards, and slept for eleven hours.

Hua looks at the streak now, bright in the silver light, and thinks: that is what a year looks like.

It is not much to see. It is not much to pay.

She looks at her own hands, folded in her lap around the end of her ribbon, and does not let herself think about what that means.

---

"You are awake," says Tamsin.

She has come up so quietly that Hua has not heard her, though the Keeper's staff rings on the boards like a struck bell. She stands at the edge of the circle with her sewn eyes turned toward the stove and a small brass kettle hanging from one hand, and she is smiling, a little, as she always does.

"I could not sleep."

"No one can, in their first night with a finished thread." The old woman lowers herself onto a stool with a creak of knees. "It is a weight. One carries it for a while, and then one learns to set it down."

"Does it get lighter?"

"No." The smile deepens. "But one gets stronger."

Hua turns her ribbon over in her hands.

It is shorter than any of the others. She knows. It is the length of her hand, no more, a narrow strip of pale blue and gold and gray, and at its end the weave changes, as Pebble's did, and Jian's, and a thread of white comes in from the side and lies down against it and stops. She has looked at the place a hundred times. She has read it like a map.

"Tamsin," she says.

"Yes."

"My thread doesn't end at the Door."

"No."

"It ends before. A hand's breadth before." She swallows. "I saw a tower. A man in the window, with his back to me. A lamp burning. I called, and he didn't turn around."

"I remember. You told us."

"I thought it meant I'd die there. At the Wall." Her voice is steady. "I thought it meant that whatever happens at the Door, I won't be there. That I'll have gone back." She looks up. "Is that what it means?"

The old Keeper is quiet for a time.

"I cannot read a thread as one reads a book," she says at last. "I can only feel its shape. It is like reading a face in the dark." She leans forward. "May I?"

Hua holds out the ribbon.

The thin dry hands take it. They pass along its length, from the bright beginning to the white, tied end, with a delicate precision that makes Hua's eyes sting. At the last hand's-breadth, they pause. They go over the place where the thread of white lies down against the blue. They go over it three times, slowly, and the old face does not change, and Hua thinks: she is lying. She is going to lie.

"It does not end," says Tamsin.

Hua's heart stops.

"It is not cut. It is not frayed. It is not a thread that has run out." The Keeper lifts her face. "It has been joined. Do you see? This white strand is not a death. It is a second thread. A thread that lies down alongside yours, and goes on."

"On where?"

"I cannot say. The Loom stops where the weaver stops." The smile is soft. "But it is a thread I have seen before. It is the kind a person weaves for another. A tie. A choosing." She returns the ribbon. "It is the thread of a Keystone's keeper."

"A keeper."

"One who holds the holder." Tamsin sets down the kettle. "I think, child, that your thread does not end at a tower. I think it ends in one. And I think that whoever is in the window, whoever has his back to you, is waiting for you to come home."

Hua cannot speak.

She sits on the boards with the ribbon pressed against her chest and her eyes burning, and the silver light slides over the long plain, and far off the looms clatter on and on.

---

Corin wakes at the second bell.

Nobody expects it. Hua is half dozing against the beam when a sound goes through the air like a dropped plate: a sharp, clean, wondering gasp, the sound of a man who has just remembered how to breathe. She starts upright. Across the platform, at the end of the row of looms, a figure in an undyed smock has fallen to its knees.

It is the weaver with the glass-bead eyes.

He kneels on the boards with his hands pressed to his face. His shoulders are shaking. He makes no sound. But as Hua watches, a drop falls between his fingers and strikes the board, and then another, and she realizes that he is weeping.

"Jian," she says, sharply.

He is already awake.

They reach the weaver at the same moment, Jian and Hua, and Veyra a pace behind, and Tamsin standing at the edge with her staff held very still. Corin does not look up. He kneels on the wood, a thin pale young man of nineteen with a vacant open face, and from behind his hands a voice comes, low and cracked and unused, like a hinge that has not moved in three hundred years.

"Thank you," he says.

Jian kneels beside him.

"For what?"

"You told me to sit." The hands come down. The eyes beneath them are wet, and brown, and no longer made of glass. "You said, you may go and sit. Nobody had said that in three hundred years. They only ever said, weave." He draws a ragged breath. "I sat. And I thought, quite suddenly: I could get up."

"And did you?"

"I'm not sure." A shaky laugh. "I'm here. I think that counts."

Tamsin's staff has gone silent on the boards.

"Corin," she says. Her voice is unsteady. "How long?"

"I do not know, Keeper. I lost count." He looks up at the sewn eyes, and a strange expression crosses his face, a compound of fear and tenderness. "You were kind to me. You gave me tea. You never asked me to talk."

"I did not want to hear what you would say."

"I know."

"It was cowardice."

"It was mercy," says Corin. "I would not have been able to answer."

For a moment, no one speaks.

Then Veyra Thann comes forward, and kneels, and puts back her hood. Her face in the silver light is gray and fine and very old. She takes the young man's chin in her ruined hand and turns his face toward her, and studies it, as a physician studies a wound.

I know you, she says.

"Lady Veyra," says Corin, faintly.

You were Orrin's apprentice.

"I was his hands, my lady. He had a tremor, in the last years. I wrote his letters." The brown eyes fill. "You came to the Door with a lantern. The night before he sealed it. I held the door for you."

I remember.

"I was nineteen." A smile like a crack in glass. "I did not know what I was holding it for."

---

He tells them over bread and cheese, in the warm light of the stove, while the Terrace turns slowly through its long silver afternoon.

He speaks haltingly at first. He has not used his voice in three hundred years, and the words come out cracked and rusty, with long gaps while he finds the next one. But he is an apprentice, and apprentices learn to remember, and the story, once it begins, runs from him like water from a cracked jar. He tells them about the Founders. He tells them about the first Orchard, and the first Loom, and the day Orrin Thann walked into the Hall of Nine with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and said, there is a way to share the burden.

"It was not a machine," he says. "Not then. It was a design. A pattern, drawn on a sheet of white skin, by a woman I never met. She had come from the first world, with the others. She was the last of the First Founders."

"Her name?" says Jian, very quietly.

"They called her the Draughtswoman. I never heard another." Corin rubs his eyes. "She drew nine seats in a ring. She drew a circle of light. She said the burden of the Door could be borne, if it were shared among nine who were willing, and if there were a single mind to bind them. A mind that could hear all nine at once and keep them in step."

Hua feels Jian go still.

"The Founders argued for a year. They said it could not be done. A mind that large would be a god, or a monster. It would not hold." Corin's voice is hoarse. "And then the Draughtswoman died. She was the first of them to go. And in her papers they found a second design."

"For what?"

"For the mind." He swallows. "A thing that could do what she described. A machine, they called it. A vessel of glass and light, no bigger than a plum. It was to be worn in the head of the Ring's chief. It would hear all nine. It would speak to them. It would keep them in step."

"The Interface," says Hua, before she can stop herself.

Everyone turns.

She feels the blood rise in her face. "I'm sorry. It's only—the Print. The Ring. Jian's—" She stops. Jian is looking at her, very steadily, with an expression she cannot read. "I've seen the way he works," she says. "I'm not stupid. I know there's something. I've never asked."

"I know," says Jian.

"I'm not asking now."

"I know." He almost smiles. "Thank you."

Corin looks from one to the other, puzzled.

"There is no such name in the papers," he says. "But the design was meant to be called by a word. Orrin put it in the margin. He wrote it in his own hand."

"What word?"

"Tenth."

The stove ticks. The silver light is very still.

---

"The Tenth," says Veyra.

Her voice is quite flat.

Of course.

"My lady?"

It was never his title. She is looking at the wall of silver mist. It was never a rank. It was the name of the machine. A breath. He called himself the Tenth because he was the one who wore it. Ninth of the nine. And tenth, with the mind. She stops. He told me he was the last. He never told me he was two.

Corin bows his head.

"He did not wear it long," he says. "A month. Perhaps less. The Ring failed. The mind could not hold. He took it out. It was a terrible thing to see, my lady. He screamed for a day. And afterward he said that the machine was too large, and too new, and that it would be a hundred years before anyone could use it."

"And then?"

"Then he lost it." The young man's voice drops. "I do not know how. It was on a table in the Hall of Nine, wrapped in a cloth. And in the morning it was gone. And the Bloom—" He swallows. "The Bloom had begun to speak."

Hua stares at him.

She feels the pieces turn in her mind, slowly, with a click like a lock. The machine was lost on the journey. That was what Orrin said, in Jian's dream. I do not know how it came to you. But the machine was not lost. It was taken. And it was taken by the one thing that could use it.

"It's been in the Bloom," she whispers. "All this time. The Interface. The thing in the Seam is wearing the other half of it."

"It can hear us," says Pebble.

He has woken. He sits against the beam with his knees drawn up and his shaven head tilted, and his eyes are wide and dark. "It can hear us, can't it? It's been listening. That's why it knew about Sun. About the sister. It heard me think it."

"It heard the Ring," says Jian slowly. "Through the leak. And now that the Ring is cut—"

"It still knows."

"It knows what it learned. It doesn't know what we say now." His face is gray. "It can only guess."

"A guess is all it needs," says Hua.

---

Her Soul wakes in the afternoon.

She is sitting alone at the edge of the platform, away from the others, with her ribbon wound round her wrist and her knees drawn up, when it happens. She has been trying to think about nothing. She has been trying to think about the sound of the looms, the smell of lavender, the shape of the silver light on the boards. And something low in her belly, below the navel, where the Core has turned for twenty years, gives a small slow flutter, like the kick of a child.

She puts her hand there.

It happens again. A tiny, clear, definite stir, a pulse that is not her own. It is not painful. It is not frightening. It is as though a bird that has been sleeping in a hollow tree has opened one eye, and looked out, and remarked on the weather.

Oh, she thinks.

She closes her eyes and turns her attention inward, the way she was taught on the Wall, and sees it.

It is very small. It is no bigger than a seed pearl, pale gold and faintly translucent, curled in the center of her dantian like a fish in a bowl. It has a face, or the beginning of one, the suggestion of two closed eyes and a small round mouth. It is breathing. It is breathing in time with her, slowly, steadily, and with each breath it grows a hair's breadth brighter.

Hello, she thinks.

The pearl does not answer. But it turns, a little, in its sleep, and settles, and she feels a warmth spread outward from it, soft and golden, through her ribs and arms and the tips of her fingers. It is the first time in weeks she has felt warm.

"It is an infant," says Veyra, softly.

She has come up behind her, silent as a shadow. Hua does not turn.

"I thought the seed would be a Soul."

It will be. In time. The cool voice is almost gentle. The Loom has done what it can. It has shown you your end, and a Soul that has seen its end can no longer be frightened of the sky. But a Soul must be born. And a birth requires tribulation.

"Here?"

No. The Terraces have a roof. There is no open sky until the Ninth. A pause. You will carry it to the Door. And when you stand in the white room, under the glass, the clouds will gather, and you will be tried.

Hua is silent.

"Tribulation," she says.

Yes.

"I've never faced it. Nobody on the Wall has. It only comes at Nascent Soul, and—" She swallows. "Nobody's gone that far."

Wenyuan has.

"Wenyuan was carried over by the Seam. It isn't the same."

No. Veyra's voice is very dry. It is a great deal worse.

Hua laughs. It is a small, helpless, wobbling sound, and it surprises her.

I have sat under that sky once, says Veyra Thann. At the Door, the night before I slept. It rained lightning for nine hours. I was not burned. She draws a breath. But I was afraid. I should like you to know that. I should like you to know that the bravest people I have ever met were all afraid, and went on.

Hua does not answer.

She leans back, very slightly, until her shoulder touches the hem of the gray cloak. Veyra does not move away. And the pearl in her belly turns again in its sleep, and breathes.

---

Yue wakes when Pebble touches her shoulder.

She does it all at once, as she does everything, with a sharp intake of breath and a hand to her sword. She sits up so fast that the white streak in her hair swings across her face. She looks about her, at the circle of stools, the iron stove, the silver plain, and her eyes find Jian.

"What?" she says.

"Corin remembered," says Jian. He has not moved from beside the weaver. "He was Orrin's apprentice. He knows what the Tenth is. Hua will tell you the rest."

"Tell me the part that matters."

"That the thing at the top of the Seam is wearing the other half of what I carry." He says it quietly. "And that every hour we spend on this Terrace is an hour it spends learning where we are."

Yue is silent for a moment. She looks at the red ribbon on Pebble's wrist, and the pale young weaver, and the small brass kettle, and the white-haired Keeper at the edge of the light.

"Then we go now," she says.

"There's a stair at the far end of the Terrace," says Tamsin. "It goes to the Seventh. I can take you."

"How far?"

"A mile."

"Then we'll be there in ten minutes." Yue gets to her feet, stiffly, favoring her right leg, and for a moment Hua thinks she will fall. But she doesn't. She stands with her stone hand at her side, tall and thin and terribly calm, and surveys the platform with the flat gray eye of a general. She turns to Pebble. "Can you carry the skin?"

"Yes, Master."

"Can you carry Corin?"

The boy blinks. "I—Master?"

"He's been a weaver for three hundred years. He doesn't know how to walk anywhere that isn't a plank bridge." A tight, bleak smile. "I'd like him to have the choice."

Corin makes a small sound.

"I can walk," he says. His voice is thin. "I am quite certain I can walk. It is only that I have not done so in a very long time."

"Then you'll start now."

She picks up her pack. She slings it over her shoulder, and settles the sword at her hip, and stands for a moment looking at the tall hooded woman in the gray cloak, and the old blind Keeper with the staff, and the thin pale boy in the undyed smock.

"Everyone's coming," she says.

It is not a question. And nobody argues. Pebble takes the weaver's thin arm and tucks it through his own, with an awkward gentleness that makes Hua look away; Veyra pulls up her hood; Tamsin sets down the brass kettle on the stove with a small final click, as one closes a door on a house one will not see again.

---

The sound begins as they are packing.

It is a small thing, at first: a thin high whine, like a wet finger drawn around the rim of a glass. Hua lifts her head. Across the platform Veyra has gone rigid, one hand pressed against her spine, and the ring of ember on her bare palm is burning white. Tamsin has risen from her stool. The kettle, forgotten in her hand, is rattling against its chain.

"Keeper?" says Jian.

"Hush."

The whine rises. It becomes a hum, a drone, a shivering in the boards under their feet. Hua feels it in her teeth. All across the vast silver plain, row on row, the looms have stopped.

Not slowed. Stopped.

For the first time since they entered the Terrace, the great clatter has ceased. The shuttles hang in the air. The weavers stand with their hands lifted, like marionettes whose strings have been cut, and in the sudden vast silence a single clear note rings out across the Sixth Terrace, high and pure and sweet.

It is a bell.

It is on the stair, says Veyra Thann. Her voice is hoarse. They are on the stair.

"Who?"

Tamsin turns her sewn eyes toward the door of pale wood, wide as a barn, standing ajar on the stair they came by. Her face is perfectly white.

"The Refused," she says. "The two million. They have come up the Road of Nine, in a single day of the world below, and they are climbing my stair."

Hua stares at her.

"That's impossible," she says. "They only left the Hall—"

"Outside, it has been a month. Here, it has been a morning." The old woman's voice is steady, and terrible. "They walk in step. They walk singing. And the Loom has begun to weave them in."

"Weave them in to what?"

Tamsin lifts her hand.

All across the plain, from every loom, from every beam and roller and frame, a thread is rising. Not the pale cool threads of the Terrace. Thick, living, brilliantly colored ropes of light, red and gold and green and violet, hundreds of thousands of them, rising from the floor and arching over the plain like the ribs of a vast tent. They are converging. They are weaving, with a speed that makes Hua's eyes ache, into a single immense cable, which hangs for a moment glowing in the air above the platform, and then plunges toward the roof.

It goes up through the silver ceiling like a spear.

The Door, says Veyra. The Loom is feeding the Door.

"The Door is weaving a new warp," says Tamsin. "It is using their threads. Every one of them. Every sleeper who said no." She lowers her hand. "It is not burning them. It is binding them. It is making them into the cloth that holds the Door shut."

"For how long?"

"Forever."

Pebble makes a small sound in his throat.

"Sun," he says.

Nobody answers.

The great cable of light hangs above them, shivering with ten thousand colors. And down the pale wooden stair, from the vast dark mouth of the door, a sound comes rising: a low, sweet, tidal murmur, like the singing of a very large and very happy crowd.
